title: Fear not, and the reason why
hookLine: fear not appears again and again in scripture
carry: fear not comes with a reason

cards: Abram, in a vision, childless and waiting. A young woman in Nazareth, with an angel in the room. Shepherds in a dark field, suddenly lit up.
Women at a tomb that should not be empty. John on the island of Patmos, falling at someone's feet as though dead. Different places, different stories, different people.
And to each of them, heaven says the same two words. Fear not.

teach.h: FEAR NOT, ABRAM: I AM THY SHIELD.
teach.b: You heard it in year two, said to a little flock. Now listen to what comes right after those words. To Abram: "Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward."
To Mary: "Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God." To the shepherds: "Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people."
To John on Patmos, with a right hand laid on him: "Fear not; I am the first and the last."
And through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, called my servant: "Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God." Hear the pattern? For.
I am. Behold. In these passages, fear not is never just a command left hanging.

teach.h: A SENTENCE WITH A SECOND HALF.
teach.b: It's a sentence with a second half, and the second half is a reason, usually a presence. And the frightened people aren't scolded.
Luke says the shepherds were "sore afraid." The angel doesn't tell them they're overreacting. It gives them news big enough to step out of the fear.
Then notice when the words come. Abram is waiting on a promise. Mary is about to say yes to something enormous.
The women at the tomb are standing at the edge of a story that's just changed.
Fear not keeps showing up at thresholds, right before something new. So in scripture, fear not doesn't pretend fear isn't there. It speaks to the fear directly, and then it gives a reason.

how: Christians often memorize fear-not verses such as Isaiah 41:10 and say them in anxious moments, and the angel's 'fear not' to the shepherds is read aloud in churches at Christmas.

o: a command to stop feeling fear by willpower
heaven's words to the afraid, with a reason given

games.q: who heard fear not — tap the pairs.
p: thou hast found favour with God
I am the first and the last

s: a Bible verse says there's a fear not for every day of the year
that's a popular saying, not a verse. the phrase comes again and again, but no verse makes that count.
the shepherds in Luke are scolded for being afraid
they were sore afraid, and the angel answered with good tidings of great joy.
in Isaiah 41, fear not comes with a reason
fear thou not; for I am with thee.

games.q: you're a shepherd in a field at night. a light surrounds you, an angel appears, and you're sore afraid. what does the angel say first?
o: you should have more faith than this.
fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy.
games.why: fear not, and then the reason: good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. the fear isn't scolded; it's answered.

practice: Let one fear come up, about money, your health, a person you love, what's coming next, and name it plainly without arguing with it.
Then say the two words to it, out loud or inside, fear not, and give it a second half the way scripture does.
If you pray, borrow Isaiah's, for I am with thee; if you don't, let the second half be something true and steady: I'm breathing, I'm here, this moment holds.

wordCard.voice: Fear not. Heaven's words to Abram, Mary, the shepherds and John, each time followed by a reason: I am, for, behold.

orig.note: Hebrew: fear not, said to one person — the words to Abram in Genesis 15:1.

carryVoice: Your line: fear not comes with a reason. The shepherds were sore afraid, and heaven answered with good news, not a scolding. See you in the morning.
